Title: Adaptive synchrosqueezing wavelet transform for real-time applications - ScienceDirect
# Adaptive synchrosqueezing wavelet transform for real-time applications. In this paper, we introduce an adaptive algorithm based on the Synchrosqueezing Wavelet Transform, aimed at implementations on systems with constrained computational power. Time-Frequency (TF) analysis is a central and mature area in non-stationary signal processing. For instance, the Time-reassigned Synchrosqueezing Transform (TSST) *squeezes* in the time domain, instead of *squeezing* in the frequency domain, making it more suitable to analyze impulsive signals [9]. In this paper, we address the problem of implementing TF analysis for these cases, in particular, for those that require real-time processing. To cope with this matter, we propose to dynamically redistribute the analysis frequencies (scales) of the Wavelet Transform (WT) to relevant areas of the signal spectrum. By doing so, the standard WT, the SST, or other TF analysis methods, such as TSST, RM, or SET, could be computed with a lower number of analysis frequencies obtaining a resolution similar to the one obtained with a larger transform. To complete the analysis, we explore different criteria for frequency grid reallocation and we test the algorithm performance by processing different types of input signals including synthetic and real-world ones. Along with the presentation, we provide an open-source Python implementation for the adaptive algorithm [24], which includes SST, TSST, RM, and SET to demonstrate the generality of the proposed method. Our aim is to perform real-time digital processing of the observed signal . In this paper, we presented a software implementation of the synchrosqueezing transform with an adaptive stage to reallocate computational resources according to signal information. Recent advances in the chirplet transform and wavelet–chirplet transform (WCT) have enabled the estimation of instantaneous frequencies (IFs) and chirprates, as well as mode retrieval from multicomponent signals with crossover IF curves. Time–frequency analysis offers an alternative approach: the synchrosqueezing transform (SST) [2] rigorously recovers components of multicomponent signals, with extensions to short-time Fourier transform (STFT)-based variants [3], [4]. To recover components with crossover instantaneous frequencies (IFs), the SSO scheme has been extended from the 2D time–frequency (or time-scale respectively) plane to 3D spaces of time–frequency– chirprate (or time–scale–chirprate respectively) using the chirplet transform (CT) [44], [45] (time–scale–chirprate transform [46] respectively). In addition, several other approaches have been put forward recently for estimating IF and/or retrieving the modes of multicomponent signals with overlapping IFs. For instance, in [51], time–frequency analysis and the Radon transform were employed, while [52] introduced a spectrogram time–frequency evolution law for estimating both IF and the chirprate. This paper proposes an X-ray transform-based wavelet–chirplet transform, termed the X-ray wavelet–chirplet transform (XWCT), which exhibits faster decay along the chirprate direction than WCT. An important task of TF analysis is to yield a sharp TF representation that energy distribution is highly concentrated at an instantaneous frequency (IF) in the TF plane. In order to yield concentrated TF representation on the premise of signal reconstruction, this article proposes a local maximum synchrosqueezing transform (LMSST)-based TF analysis method with time-varying window and time-varying searching region. In particular, the adaptive window with the time-varying function is employed to suppress the violation produced by time-varying frequency characteristics. Here, the time-varying function is optimized based on the local Rényi entropy. Also, the local maximum of the TF coefficients is computed within the time-varying region to be the estimator of the IF of the signals. The time-varying region is employed to match different kinds of signals. In the meantime, it is proved that the signals can be reconstructed. Also, reconstructed signals are closer to the origin signals. In addition, the effectiveness of the proposed method is validated on real-world signals that contain the stationary signals and the N-S signals.
